tasks.title: Mixed exam — Substation parameter sweep
tasks.context: Lines $f_k(x)=x+k$ slide vertically against $g(x)=x^{2}-2x-5$. Decide which inequalities on $k$ force two meetings, tangency, or a miss. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Exactly one value of $k$ gives tangency, namely $k=-\frac{29}{4}$.
Whenever $k<-\frac{29}{4}$, the line meets the parabola twice.
Whenever $k>-\frac{30}{4}$, the line meets the parabola twice.
When $k=2$ the line meets the parabola twice.
For every real $k$ the line meets the parabola.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Sliding the line vertically changes only the constant term of the difference, so the discriminant comes out linear in the shift:

$$g(x)-f_k(x)=x^{2}-3x-\left(5+k\right)$$

$$\Delta(k)=\left(-3\right)^{2}-4\left(-5-k\right)$$

$$\Delta(k)=4 k + 29$$

A linear expression vanishes at exactly one place:

$$4k+29=0$$

$$k=-\frac{29}{4}$$

One shift and no other makes the discriminant zero, which is one touching point, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Below the tangency threshold the discriminant is negative, and a negative discriminant means no meeting at all:

$$\Delta(k)=4 k + 29$$

$$k<-\frac{29}{4}\Rightarrow\Delta(k)<0$$

Taking a shift from that range shows it:

$$\Delta(-10)=-11$$

No real abscissa then satisfies $g(x)=f_k(x)$, so the line misses the parabola entirely rather than cutting it twice, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Two crossings need a positive discriminant, and that fixes the threshold exactly:

$$\Delta(k)=4 k + 29$$

$$\Delta(k)>0\Leftrightarrow k>-\frac{29}{4}$$

The threshold quoted in the claim is the smaller number $-\frac{30}{4}$, so its range also admits shifts between the two values. Test one:

$$\Delta\left(-\frac{59}{8}\right)=-\frac{1}{2}$$

There the line misses the parabola completely, so the claim fails on part of its own range, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Substitute the shift into the discriminant that was set up for the family:

$$\Delta(k)=4 k + 29$$

$$\Delta(2)=37$$

A positive value means the difference has two distinct real zeros, and the difference itself confirms the shape:

$$x^{2} - 3 x - 7=0$$

Two distinct real abscissae are two crossings, exactly as claimed, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Whether the line reaches the parabola depends on the shift, so the word "every" is the part to test:

$$\Delta(k)=4 k + 29$$

The discriminant is negative for all shifts below the threshold:

$$k<-\frac{29}{4}$$

One explicit counterexample settles it:

$$\Delta(-8)=-3$$

For that shift the difference has no real zero, so those two graphs never touch, so the statement is False.

tasks.title: Mixed exam — Velodrome reconstruction
tasks.context: Rebuild: line slope $2$, point $\left(3,8\right)$; parabola axis $x=3$, vertex height $-3$, lead $1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rebuilt line is $f(x)=2 x + 2$, matching the sparse point-slope data.
Rewriting $g$ in powers of the rebuilt line gives $g(x)=A f(x)^2+B f(x)+C$ with $A=\frac{1}{4}$.
The same rewrite has leading coefficient $A=\frac{5}{4}$.
The rebuilt curves meet in exactly 3 distinct real points, and the vertex height is $-3$ (not $-1$).
The axis of the rebuilt parabola is $x=4$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A slope and one point determine a line: keep the slope and let the point fix the intercept.

$$y=2x+q$$

$$8=2\cdot 3+q$$

$$q=2$$

So the line is $f(x)=2 x + 2$. Substituting the given abscissa checks it:

$$f\left(3\right)=8$$

The rebuilt formula reproduces the point with the stated slope, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Writing $g$ in powers of the line is coefficient matching, and only the squared terms decide $A$. Square the line first:

$$f(x)^{2}=4 x^{2} + 8 x + 4$$

Nothing else on the right-hand side is quadratic, so the squared terms have to agree on their own:

$$4A=1$$

$$A=\frac{1}{4}$$

The linear and constant coefficients then fix the other two numbers and the rewrite closes:

$$g(x)=\frac{1}{4}f(x)^{2}-4f(x)+13$$

The leading coefficient of the rewrite is $\frac{1}{4}$, as claimed, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Only the squared terms matter for the leading coefficient of the rewrite, so compare them directly:

$$f(x)^{2}=4 x^{2} + 8 x + 4$$

$$A\cdot 4x^{2}=x^{2}$$

$$A=\frac{1}{4}$$

Testing the claimed value shows the mismatch at once:

$$\frac{5}{4}\cdot 4x^{2}=5x^{2}$$

That would describe a parabola five times as steep as the rebuilt one, whose squared term is plain $x^{2}$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The vertex height in the claim is correct, so the count is what has to be tested. Subtract the line from the parabola:

$$g(x)-f(x)=x^{2} - 8 x + 4$$

$$\Delta=\left(-8\right)^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 4$$

$$\Delta=48$$

A positive discriminant means two distinct real crossings, and a quadratic difference cannot supply a third. The height does check out:

$$g\left(3\right)=-3$$

A correct height cannot rescue a wrong count, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The axis runs through the vertex, and the rebuild data name that vertex outright:

$$V=\left(3,-3\right)$$

The rebuilt coefficients say the same thing:

$$x=-\frac{-6}{2\cdot 1}$$

$$x=3$$

If the mirror were the claimed $x=4$, heights at equal distances from it would agree, and they do not:

$$g\left(3\right)=-3$$

$$g\left(5\right)=1$$

The axis is $x=3$, not $x=4$, so the statement is False.

tasks.title: Mixed exam — DockCrane nesting
tasks.context: A line $f(x)=3 x + 3$ and parabola $g(x)=x^{2} - 8 x + 7$ are nested in both orders. Track highest powers, leads, and a sample value. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $g(f(x))$ has highest power $x^{2}$ with leading coefficient $9$, while $f(g(x))$ has highest power $x^{2}$ with leading coefficient $3$.
$g(f(x))$ has highest power $x^{3}$ because degrees add.
There exist $A,B,C$ with $g(x)=A f(x)^2+B f(x)+C$ and $A=\frac{1}{9}$.
$f(g(3))$ always equals $g(f(3))$ for every linear $f$ and quadratic $g$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Composition substitutes one formula into the other, so expand both orders before comparing. First the line inside the parabola:

$$g(f(x))=\left(3 x + 3\right)^{2}-8\left(3 x + 3\right)+7$$

$$g(f(x))=9 x^{2} - 6 x - 8$$

Now the parabola inside the line, where the outer formula only scales and shifts what it receives:

$$f(g(x))=3\left(x^{2} - 8 x + 7\right)+3$$

$$f(g(x))=3 x^{2} - 24 x + 24$$

Both compositions are quadratic, with leading coefficients $9$ and $3$ as claimed, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Degrees add when polynomials are multiplied; under substitution they multiply, and here one of the two degrees is $1$. Expanding shows where the highest power comes from:

$$g(f(x))=\left(3 x + 3\right)^{2}-8\left(3 x + 3\right)+7$$

$$g(f(x))=9 x^{2} - 6 x - 8$$

The only square in play is the square of a linear expression:

$$\left(3 x + 3\right)^{2}=9 x^{2} + 18 x + 9$$

That reaches $x^{2}$ and stops, and no other term in $g$ raises the power, so there is no cubic term to be had, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Rewriting $g$ in powers of $f$ is coefficient matching, and the squared term alone fixes $A$. Square the line:

$$f(x)^{2}=9 x^{2} + 18 x + 9$$

Only $A f(x)^{2}$ can produce a squared term, since $B f(x)+C$ is linear, so match the two squared terms:

$$9A=1$$

$$A=\frac{1}{9}$$

The linear and constant coefficients then determine the other two numbers and the rewrite closes:

$$g(x)=\frac{1}{9}f(x)^{2}-\frac{10}{3}f(x)+16$$

Such $A$, $B$, $C$ exist and $A=\frac{1}{9}$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Both sides are single evaluations, so work from the inside out and keep the two orders apart. Line first, then parabola:

$$f\left(3\right)=12$$

$$g\left(12\right)=55$$

Now the other order, parabola first:

$$g\left(3\right)=-8$$

$$f\left(-8\right)=-21$$

Both numbers land where the claim says, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Composition is not symmetric: the inner formula acts first, so swapping the order changes what gets substituted. The stem's own pair already disagrees at $x=3$:

$$g(f(3))=55$$

$$f(g(3))=-21$$

A single pair where the two orders differ is enough to refute a claim about every line and every parabola:

$$55\neq -21$$

Equality can happen for special pairs, but not for every pair, so the statement is False.

tasks.title: Mixed exam — GlacierTour factored read
tasks.context: The parabola is written $g(x)=2x(x-4)$ and the line is $f(x)=1 - x$. Watch Vieta sign traps and the midpoint rule for the axis. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The zeros read from the factors are $x=0$ and $x=4$.
By Vieta on the expanded form, the root sum equals $4$ and therefore the axis is $x=2$.
The axis of symmetry is $x=3$ because one root is shifted by one unit.
The product of the roots equals $0$ (sign flipped from $c/a$).
At the left-hand zero $x=0$, the signed gap $f-g$ equals $1$, and the graphs meet in exactly 2 real points overall.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A product is zero exactly when one of its factors is zero, so the factored form hands over the zeros with no expansion at all:

$$x=0$$

$$x-4=0$$

The two abscissae are $0$ and $4$. Substituting either one collapses the whole product:

$$g\left(0\right)=0$$

$$g\left(4\right)=0$$

Those are exactly the zeros named, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Expanding puts the coefficients where Vieta can reach them:

$$g(x)=2 x^{2} - 8 x$$

$$x_{1}+x_{2}=-\frac{-8}{2}$$

$$x_{1}+x_{2}=4$$

The axis bisects the zeros, so halving that sum gives it:

$$\frac{4}{2}=2$$

Root sum $4$ and axis $x=2$, both as claimed, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The axis sits midway between the zeros, so it is their average and not a root shifted by hand:

$$\frac{0+4}{2}=2$$

Sliding it one unit to $x=3$ would demand that heights at equal distances either side of that line agree. They do not:

$$g\left(2\right)=-8$$

$$g\left(4\right)=0$$

Only $x=2$ folds the curve onto itself, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Vieta reads the product off the expanded coefficients:

$$g(x)=2 x^{2} - 8 x$$

$$x_{1}x_{2}=\frac{0}{2}$$

$$x_{1}x_{2}=0$$

The factored form agrees, because one of the zeros is the origin:

$$0\cdot 4=0$$

Flipping the sign of zero changes nothing, so the number named is right either way, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Two things to settle: the signed gap at a named abscissa, and the total number of crossings. At the left-hand zero the parabola is on the horizontal axis, so the gap is just the height of the line:

$$g\left(0\right)=0$$

$$f\left(0\right)=1$$

$$f\left(0\right)-g\left(0\right)=1$$

For the crossings, subtract and count real zeros:

$$g(x)-f(x)=2 x^{2} - 7 x - 1$$

$$\Delta=57$$

A positive discriminant gives two crossings, so both halves hold, so the statement is True.

tasks.title: Mixed exam — BalloonFest hybrid check
tasks.context: BalloonFest supplies both a sparse table and a figure for $f(x)=5 x - 4$, $g(x)=- x^{2} - 12 x + 2$. Each letter uses a different evidence channel. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: (Graph) The vertex sits at $\left(-6,38\right)$.
(Table) The gap $f-g$ at $x=2$ equals $32$.
(Algebra) Rewrite coefficient $A$ equals $\frac{24}{25}$.
(Meetings) Discriminant of $g-f$ gives exactly 2 real intersections.
(Nesting) $g(f(x))$ has degree $3$ because a parabola wraps a line.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The turning point follows from the coefficients of $g$, and the figure only has to agree with them. The axis first:

$$x=-\frac{-12}{2\left(-1\right)}$$

$$x=-6$$

Then the height at that abscissa:

$$g\left(-6\right)=-\left(-6\right)^{2}-12\left(-6\right)+2$$

$$g\left(-6\right)=38$$

The vertex is $\left(-6,38\right)$, exactly the point named, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The table supplies both values at $x=2$, so the gap is a subtraction in the order named, $f$ minus $g$:

$$f(2)=6$$

$$g(2)=-26$$

$$f(2)-g(2)=32$$

The formulas confirm both tabulated entries:

$$5\cdot 2-4=6$$

$$-\left(2\right)^{2}-12\left(2\right)+2=-26$$

The signed gap is $32$, as claimed, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The rewrite coefficient is fixed by the squared terms alone, so square the line and compare:

$$f(x)^{2}=25 x^{2} - 40 x + 16$$

Only $A f(x)^{2}$ can produce a squared term, so it must match the squared term of $g$:

$$25A=-1$$

$$A=-\frac{1}{25}$$

The claimed value has the wrong sign as well as the wrong size, and it would make the rewrite open upwards:

$$\frac{24}{25}\cdot 25x^{2}=24x^{2}$$

The coefficient is $-\frac{1}{25}$, not $\frac{24}{25}$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Intersections are the real zeros of the difference, so subtract and take the discriminant:

$$g(x)-f(x)=-x^{2} - 17 x + 6$$

$$\Delta=\left(-17\right)^{2}-4\left(-1\right)\cdot 6$$

$$\Delta=313$$

A positive discriminant gives two distinct real zeros, hence two crossings, exactly as claimed, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Wrapping a parabola around a line multiplies the two degrees instead of adding them, and one of them is $1$. Expanding settles it:

$$g(f(x))=-\left(5 x - 4\right)^{2}-12\left(5 x - 4\right)+2$$

$$g(f(x))=-25 x^{2} - 20 x + 34$$

No term can climb past $x^{2}$, because the only square in play is the square of a linear expression:

$$\left(5 x - 4\right)^{2}=25 x^{2} - 40 x + 16$$

The composition is quadratic, not cubic, so the statement is False.

tasks.title: Mixed exam — PortPilot dense scenarios
tasks.context: Chapter 7 mixed exam — PortPilot batch 3. Each statement below is its own mini-scenario about lines or parabolas; no shared stem formulas. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: (i) For $p(x)=5 x^{2} - 3 x + 3$, the axis is $x=\frac{3}{10}$ and the vertex height is $\frac{51}{20}$.
(ii) A line with slope $3$ through $\left(2,11\right)$ is $y=3 x + 5$, but shifting the intercept by $1$ would still pass through the point.
(iii) For $q(x)=- 3 x^{2} + 8 x - 4$, the vertex occurs at $x=2$ with height $4$.
(iv) With $f(x)=x + 3$ and $g(x)=x \left(2 x - 5\right)$, the composition $g(f(x))$ has degree $3$.
(v) The roots of $x^{2} - 10 x + 21=0$ multiply to $-21$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Scenario (i) asks for the axis and the turning height of one parabola. The axis comes from the first two coefficients:

$$x=-\frac{-3}{2\cdot 5}$$

$$x=\frac{3}{10}$$

Substituting that abscissa gives the height:

$$p\left(\frac{3}{10}\right)=5\left(\frac{3}{10}\right)^{2}-3\left(\frac{3}{10}\right)+3$$

$$p\left(\frac{3}{10}\right)=\frac{51}{20}$$

Axis $\frac{3}{10}$ and height $\frac{51}{20}$ are the two numbers claimed, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Scenario (ii) has a correct first half and a false second half. The slope and the point fix the intercept:

$$11=3\cdot 2+q$$

$$q=5$$

So $y=3x+5$ is right. Shifting the intercept by one unit gives a parallel line, and parallel lines with different intercepts have no point in common:

$$y=3x+6$$

$$3\cdot 2+6=12$$

That height is $12$, not the $11$ the point requires, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

Scenario (iii) names an abscissa that is not the axis of this parabola. Compute it from the coefficients:

$$x=-\frac{8}{2\left(-3\right)}$$

$$x=\frac{4}{3}$$

The height at the genuine vertex is not the claimed number either:

$$q\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)=\frac{4}{3}$$

At the abscissa the claim quotes, the curve is on the horizontal axis:

$$q\left(2\right)=0$$

Neither the abscissa nor the height matches, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Scenario (iv) substitutes a line into a parabola, and substitution multiplies the degrees instead of adding them. Replace $x$ by the line inside $g$:

$$g(f(x))=\left(x + 3\right)\left(2\left(x + 3\right)-5\right)$$

$$g(f(x))=2 x^{2} + 7 x + 3$$

The factored form makes the same point: a product of two linear factors is quadratic.

$$g(f(x))=\left(x + 3\right) \left(2 x + 1\right)$$

The highest power is $x^{2}$, so the composition is quadratic rather than cubic, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Scenario (v) is a Vieta sign trap. For a monic quadratic the product of the roots is the constant term itself, with no sign change:

$$x_{1}x_{2}=\frac{21}{1}$$

$$x_{1}x_{2}=21$$

Factoring confirms it, since the roots can be read off directly:

$$x^{2} - 10 x + 21=\left(x-3\right)\left(x-7\right)$$

$$3\cdot 7=21$$

The product is $21$, not $-21$, so the statement is False.
